newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa labour says strikes to start Monday.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa labour says strikes to start Monday.

text.p: South Africa's largest trade union federation, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), said on Friday regional strikes would start on Monday to protest at a controversial new employment bill.
A Cosatu spokesman told state radio there had been no breakthrough on the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill in a last ditch meeting with the African National Congress (ANC) on Thursday night.
"There was no resolution and proposals made will be discussed at a special meeting next Thursday," he said.
Cosatu official Noweto Mpati reaffirmed earlier on Friday that Cosatu would continue its campaign of "rolling mass action" over the bill.
"We're definitely going ahead next week with our mass action programme," she told Reuters.
Government's inability to reach agreement with labour means the first of a series of deadlines set by Labour Minister Tito Mboweni has been missed.
He had said broad consensus had to be reached between labour and business by August 15 to ensure that the bill could be adopted by parliament this year.

A labour ministry spokeswoman declined to comment on the outcome of the talks on Friday, but confirmed the government would be involved in further negotiations with labour and business over the weekend.
The two million member Cosatu federation has staged escalating protests over the past two months to push for its demands over the bill to be met.
On June 2 it staged a national strike followed by a one-hour national work stoppage on August 1. From August 18 to 21, Cosatu plans 24-hour strikes in each of the country's nine provinces.

Labour and business have been at loggerheads over core demands relating to a reduced working week, maternity leave, overtime rates, Sunday work and the variation of employment standards in specific circumstances.
Cosatu has said there will be no compromise on its demands for six months maternity leave, of which four should be paid, and a 40-hour working week within five years.
Business has agreed to a reduction in the working week from 46 to 45 hours, but rejectes the inclusion in the bill of a commitment to a 40-hour working week.
Mboweni told reporters this week a study conducted by his department concluded that a 45-hour week would be appropriate for South Africa as a developing country.
Business also is unhappy about proposals to increase the minimum overtime rate from time-and-a-third to time-and-a-half and provisions for three days "family responsibility" leave.
Mboweni told Reuters recently the bill could "wither away" if it is not adopted before parliament begins a Christmas recess in November.
